Overtime reference

Overtime Rules by State

Daily overtime exists in only five states. See which states pay overtime after 8, 10, or 12 hours in a day, which states use the federal 40-hour weekly rule, and where the weekly threshold itself differs.

The federal baseline

Under the federal Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA), non-exempt employees earn at least one and one-half times their regular rate for hours over 40 in a workweek. The FLSA has no daily trigger: a 14-hour day earns no federal overtime if the week's total stays at or below 40 hours. It also requires no premium for weekend or holiday work by itself — only hours over the weekly threshold create overtime. A workweek is a fixed, recurring 168-hour period the employer sets; hours cannot be averaged across two weeks.

State rules stack on top of the federal rule. When both a state rule and the federal rule apply to the same hours, the employer owes whichever calculation produces the higher pay.

States with daily overtime

Only five states require daily overtime for most workers. Every other state uses the weekly rule only, unless a contract or union agreement adds more.

StateDaily triggerRateWho it covers
AlaskaOver 8 hours in a day1.5×Most hourly workers; employers with 4 or more employees
CaliforniaOver 8 hours in a day; over 12 hours in a day1.5×, then 2×All non-exempt workers; also 2× after 8 hours on the 7th consecutive day
ColoradoOver 12 hours in a day, or 12 consecutive hours1.5×Whichever pays more: the daily or the weekly calculation
NevadaOver 8 hours in a day1.5×Only employees earning less than 1.5× the state minimum wage
OregonOver 10 hours in a day1.5×Mill, factory, and manufacturing workers only (8 hours for timber and sawmill work)

Statutes: Alaska Stat. § 23.10.060 · Cal. Lab. Code § 510 · 7 Colo. Code Regs. § 1103-1 · Nev. Rev. Stat. § 608.018 · Or. Rev. Stat. § 652.020.

A worked example (California)

At $22 an hour, four 10-hour shifts total 40 hours. Under the federal weekly rule alone, there is no overtime: 40 × $22 = $880.

California counts daily overtime too. Each 10-hour day has 2 daily overtime hours, so the week pays 32 straight-time hours × $22 = $704, plus 8 daily overtime hours × $33 = $264, for $968 — $88 more than the federal calculation, in a week that never passed 40 hours.

States where the weekly threshold differs

Two states write a higher weekly threshold into state law: Kansas sets overtime after 46 hours in a week, and Minnesota after 48 hours (Minn. Stat. § 177.25).

For most workers this changes nothing. Both states' higher thresholds mainly cover workers the FLSA does not reach; if your employer is covered by the FLSA — as most are — the federal 40-hour rule governs, because the employer must satisfy whichever law pays you more. The 46- and 48-hour thresholds matter mostly for small employers and workers outside federal coverage.

Other state rules worth knowing

Kentucky has no daily overtime, but it has a seventh-day rule: under KRS 337.050, an employee who works all seven days of a workweek is paid time and a half for the seventh day's hours, unless the week's total is 40 hours or fewer. Supervisors and a few other roles are excluded.

A few more states have daily rules for specific jobs only — not general coverage. Florida requires daily overtime after 10 hours for manual laborers, and Hawaii, New York, Rhode Island, and Washington require it after 8 hours on public works projects. If you do not work those jobs, the weekly rule is the one that applies to you.

In the remaining states, overtime means the federal rule: 1.5× after 40 hours in a week, with no daily trigger and no weekend premium required by law.

What this means for the overtime calculator

Our overtime calculator uses the weekly model: it prices hours over 40 in a week at time and a half. If you work in Alaska, California, Colorado, Nevada, or Oregon, your actual overtime can be higher than the weekly calculation — check the table above for the daily trigger that applies to you.

Common questions

Does my state have daily overtime?

Only five states have daily overtime for most workers: Alaska, California, Colorado, Nevada, and Oregon — and Nevada limits its rule by wage level while Oregon limits its rule to manufacturing work. In the other 45 states there is no general daily trigger, though a few have their own twists — Kentucky's seventh-day rule and the higher weekly thresholds in Kansas and Minnesota — covered above.

Do I get overtime for working weekends or holidays?

Not under federal law. The FLSA requires no premium for Saturdays, Sundays, or holidays by themselves — only hours over 40 in a week, or a state daily or seventh-day trigger, create overtime. Any weekend premium comes from your employer, a contract, or a state rule for specific jobs.

When a state rule and the federal rule both apply, which one wins?

The one that pays you more. Employers must run both calculations and owe whichever produces the higher pay for that week.

General information, not legal advice. Overtime rules change, and exemptions for executive, administrative, professional, and other roles can remove coverage entirely. Check your state labor agency for the current rule.
